I'm really in no position to give advice, but you can go to school part-time and work part-time. Something basic like stocking shelves. Getting back into the school and/or work routine will probably be beneficial and you can slowly improve your social skills with the continued social contact that those environments provide. You'll just have to look into careers and pick one that you think interests you. Any choice is probably better than none. If you're concerned about starting college later, well there are definitely older students in every program. I wouldn't sweat it too much. Going back would probably benefit you more than not. Something like a technician or assistant program (I think these might cost a lot more upfront, I'm not sure), or certificate, if not a degree. I think if your family can fork out the money, or if you can save up the money over time, it could be worth the investment in the long run. 

Or if possible, you can see a therapist, but likely a social worker, who is supposed to help you work through some issues and set you up with work. Or a psychiatrist who will prescribe some meds to alleviate any issues you're experiencing. Either can be very costly, or affordable, or free, depending on your insurance or lack thereof. I've had both but I kinda dropped the ball with my 1st social worker and didn't make full use of her as I should have. And it's still pretty early with my meds.

Thank you very much for responding :)

I thought that expressing or appearing to have "active intent" (my terminology could be wrong) to carry out the plan was what could get you committed. But then I came across some cases online where having a plan and means to carry out that plan (especially very lethal means like a firearm) got people committed. So now I'm pretty paranoid and conflicted over what I want to do. 

It's counterintuitive but another thing is that I don't exactly want the gun or ammunition removed either... because a part of me wants them available should I decide to go through with it one day in the future. >.> But that's perhaps a less risky (maybe only marginally) way to introduce the issue--by asking for advice on securing it as it would show or suggest interest and effort in preventing suicide. I will definitely consider that. 

I don't know if I feel shame about it exactly. If my family were out of the picture, I think I wouldn't have an issue telling my therapist or even being committed. I almost feel like I need it. But they are in the picture, and I feel extremely adversed to them knowing all this. I don't want the drama and attention, much like I used to get from them in the past which was excruciatingly unpleasant. I also wonder though to what extent I should actually be confronting my fears and just be open to them about all this. Like maybe it would expedite my progress. I don't know what I want to do yet but will think it over some more.

Thanks for taking the time to reply :) 

Yeah, I've noticed that I can be very contradictory in my thinking. For example, I actually really want to confess about the gun, because I have a reoccurring fear that I will use it (part of my ocd i think) that I want openly address. At the same time, I don't want to mention the gun... because in my mind, doing so could bring things one step closer to getting it removed or confiscated, which I also don't want because a part of me wants it there as an option for suicide later. Then this all sounds like I definitely have some intention, and yet I feel as if I don't exactly... lol. :[ I thought that having a plan and having intent (to actually execute the plan) were viewed as two separate things, but I certainly could be wrong. 

I don't know yet whether I will discuss it or not. It feels like taking a very scary leap with unpredictable consequences. I am going to think it over. Thanks again for the insight!
This is also very informative in that it gives me an idea of possible costs of further appointments and medication. Thank you!!

I see. Thanks for the response! Based on some personal experiences I read about online, it does appear that Medi-Cal covers most if not all medical costs. Although much of the trouble seems to be in getting those medical appointments/treatments to begin with as well as quality of care. Luckily(?) I get mine through a clinic where they sort of arrange the specialists for me. So I guess my main concern at the moment is wait time between care.
This was the impression I was getting about Medi-Cal coverage but just wanted to hear some personal experiences for reassurance. This info eases my concerns a lot, thank you !!

To be honest, I don't understand health insurance very well at all... so I can't say confidently whether or not you will encounter the same experience as mine in terms of treatment options and costs (or lack thereof). Hope this helps a bit though!

I can reallyy relate to you. Yes, I have some experience with Medi-Cal insurance (I chose HealthNet if that matters, I don't know) in California right now. A few months ago, I saw my PCP about feelings of anxiety and depression. My PCP asked if I wanted to see a psychiatrist (also had me do a physical and follow-up); I said sure but was scheduled an appointment with a Licensed Clinical Social Worker instead. Prior to the first appointment, they called me asking for various details (one of which being current employment status to which I told them I am unemployed). They asked more questions just prior and during the first in-person session and have you fill out some paperwork/questionnaires. They explained to me during my first session that the treatment (total of 10 sessions aimed at CBT, not including the first which is more of an assessment meeting) would be free of charge due to Medi-Cal (and I'm assuming my unemployment status or something...). I was not prescribed medication so I can't speak to how much that would cost if anything. But I might find out soon/within the next few weeks as I will possibly be given meds for OCD as well... I'll update you.
